title: Ethiopian Berbere Oil
community: Ethiopian fasting kitchens — berbere without kibbeh
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Berbere Oil — vegetable oil infused with berbere, garlic, and onion over low heat. The vegan alternative to kibbeh — used during fasting periods to provide the fat-soluble colour and flavour of berbere without dairy.
longDesc: Berbere oil is the fasting cook's essential tool — it provides the same function as kibbeh (fat that dissolves the berbere's fat-soluble carotenoids and distributes their colour throughout the wat) without any animal products.
steps: Combine oil, berbere, garlic, and onion in a small saucepan.
Heat over the lowest possible flame for 12—15 minutes.
The oil should never fry — just gently warm and infuse.
Cool. Strain through a fine sieve.
The resulting red oil is used as the fat base for all fasting wats.
chefTips: The lowest possible heat — this is infusing, not frying.
Strain completely — leave no solids in the oil.
The red colour is the quality indicator — deeper red = better berbere.
commonMistakes: Too high heat — fries the berbere instead of infusing.
cookingScience: Berbere's carotenoids (fat-soluble pigments responsible for the red colour) dissolve readily into oil at gentle temperatures. Unlike water, which cannot dissolve these pigments, oil extracts them completely — producing the characteristic red oil that colours and flavours the entire fasting wat.
sustainabilityTips: Sunflower or rapeseed oil — the most widely available neutral oils in Ethiopia.
servedWith: As the fat base for all fasting wats
As a condiment drizzled over fasting dishes
storage: Sealed jar at room temperature — 3 months. Refrigerate for longer.
healthBenefits: Carotenoids from berbere extracted into a bioavailable fat form.
culturalNote: Berbere oil is the invisible hero of Ethiopian fasting cuisine — the vegan fat that makes Misir Wat red, that makes Shiro Wat fragrant, and that makes the entire fasting platter as visually vibrant as its meat-day equivalent.
